common_name: Parks' Yellow Tea-Scented China Rose (Historic Stud Rose, Ancestor of Yellow Roses)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root, own-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Parks' Yellow was brought from China to England in 1824 and is one of the four original 'stud China' roses that introduced yellow coloring and tea fragrance into Western rose breeding.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun, ideally with support or a wall to lean on, as Parks' Yellow produces long, sprawling, semi-climbing canes. Introduced to England from China in 1824, it is one of the four historic 'stud China' roses whose genes underpin nearly all modern yellow and tea-scented roses, bearing loosely double, pale sulphur-yellow flowers that fade toward cream as they age. Bloom can be shy and uneven compared with modern repeat-flowering roses, reflecting its status as a foundational breeding parent rather than a polished garden performer, but it tolerates Gulf Coast heat and humidity well once established. Prune only to remove dead or crossing wood, since heavy cutting back reduces the sparse bloom further.

common_name: Hume's Blush Tea-Scented China Rose (Historic Stud Rose, Ancestor of Tea Fragrance)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root, own-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Hume's Blush was introduced to England around 1809, named for Sir Abraham Hume, and is one of the four original 'stud China' roses credited with bringing true tea fragrance into Western rose breeding.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Introduced to England from China around 1809 and named for Sir Abraham Hume, this is one of the four historic 'stud China' roses whose introduction revolutionized Western rose breeding by contributing the true tea scent and repeat-blooming habit found in later tea and hybrid tea roses. Its pale blush-pink, loosely double flowers carry a light, classic tea fragrance and open over a long season rather than in the single flush typical of old European roses. Like other antique Chinas it tolerates heat, humidity, and poor soil far better than modern hybrid teas. Needs only light pruning to remove dead or crossing wood, as it is grown today chiefly for historic interest and breeding heritage rather than for a dramatic floral display.

common_name: Madame Laurette Messimy Rose (Antique Peach-Pink China Rose)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root, own-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Madame Laurette Messimy, introduced by Guillot in France in 1887, is a China rose valued for its unusual peach-pink, copper-tinged blooms and nearly continuous flowering.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Introduced in France in 1887, Madame Laurette Messimy bears loosely semi-double flowers in a changeable blend of peachy pink, salmon, and coppery tones that shift with temperature and light, opening almost continuously from spring to frost. Like other old China roses it is notably tolerant of heat, humidity, and lean soil, performing reliably in the Gulf South with minimal care. Its relatively compact, bushy habit suits mixed borders and foundation plantings as well as historic rose collections. Prune lightly after flushes to tidy growth and encourage continued rebloom.

common_name: Pompon de Paris Rose (Miniature Antique China Rose)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root, own-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Pompon de Paris is a diminutive antique China rose long cultivated in pots on Parisian balconies and market stalls in the 19th century, now considered an ancestor of modern miniature roses.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; this tiny antique China rose performs especially well in containers, where its compact mounding habit and fine-textured foliage can be shown off at close range. Long grown in 19th-century France as a potted balcony and market plant, it bears small, fully double, rose-pink pompon-shaped flowers in dense flushes nearly continuously through the growing season. It shares the heat and humidity tolerance typical of old China roses and needs little more than occasional light shaping and deadheading of spent blooms to keep flowering steadily.

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root, own-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Fabvier, introduced in 1832, is a compact antique China rose bearing bright crimson-red flowers often splashed or streaked with white.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Introduced in 1832, Fabvier is a compact, bushy China rose bearing semi-double, bright red flowers frequently marked or streaked with white, set against small, dark green foliage on a plant that stays notably low and tidy for an old China rose. It flowers in repeated flushes from spring to frost and, like other antique Chinas, tolerates heat, humidity, and poor soil far better than modern roses, having long persisted at old homesites with no care. Prune lightly after bloom flushes to remove spent wood and maintain its compact form.

common_name: Duchesse de Montebello Rose (Antique Soft Pink Gallica)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Duchesse de Montebello, raised by Jean Laffay in France in the 1820s, is a refined Gallica rose with soft pink, fully double flowers.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Duchesse de Montebello tolerates leaner soil and more neglect than modern hybrid tea roses, in keeping with its heritage as a tough antique Gallica. Raised by the French breeder Jean Laffay in the 1820s, it bears fully double, softly cupped flowers in a delicate pale pink, carried in elegant, slightly nodding clusters with a sweet, refined fragrance. Like other Gallicas it blooms once in a heavy late-spring flush and then rests for the remainder of the season, but is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy. Needs only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering to stay vigorous and well-shaped.

common_name: Assemblage des Beautes Rose (Antique Bright Crimson-Pink Gallica)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Assemblage des Beautes, an early-19th-century Gallica, bears vivid crimson-pink flowers with a neat button eye.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Assemblage des Beautes tolerates leaner soil and more neglect than modern hybrid tea roses, in keeping with its heritage as a tough antique Gallica. Dating to the early 1800s, it bears intensely fragrant, fully double flowers that open a vivid crimson-pink to cerise, fading only slightly as they age and usually forming a neat button eye at the center. Like other Gallicas it blooms once in a dramatic late-spring flush and then rests for the remainder of the season, but is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy. Needs only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering to stay vigorous and well-shaped.

common_name: Alain Blanchard Rose (Antique Mottled Purple-Red Gallica)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Alain Blanchard, bred by Jean-Pierre Vibert and introduced in 1811, is a Gallica rose noted for its semi-double flowers heavily mottled and spotted with deep purple and maroon.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Alain Blanchard tolerates leaner soil and more neglect than modern hybrid tea roses, in keeping with its heritage as a tough antique Gallica. Bred by the French rose breeder Jean-Pierre Vibert and introduced in 1811, it bears semi-double flowers that open purplish-red and are heavily splashed, spotted, and mottled with deeper maroon and purple, maturing to a smoky plum color and set off by prominent golden stamens. Like other Gallicas it blooms once in a heavy late-spring flush and then rests for the remainder of the season, but is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy. Needs only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering to stay vigorous and well-shaped.

common_name: President de Seze Rose (Antique Bicolor Magenta-and-Lilac Gallica)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; President de Seze is an old Gallica rose, in cultivation since before the mid-1800s, prized for its striking two-toned flowers.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; President de Seze tolerates leaner soil and more neglect than modern hybrid tea roses, in keeping with its heritage as a tough antique Gallica. One of the most striking old Gallicas, it bears large, fully double flowers with a vivid magenta-pink to cerise center that fades sharply to pale lilac-gray on the outer petals, creating a bold two-toned effect, carried with a strong classic fragrance. Like other Gallicas it blooms once in a heavy late-spring flush and then rests for the remainder of the season, but is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy. Needs only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering to stay vigorous and well-shaped.

common_name: Paul Ricault Rose (Antique Rose-Pink Centifolia Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Paul Ricault, introduced in France in 1845, is a Centifolia hybrid with large, very double, rose-pink globular flowers.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Paul Ricault tolerates leaner soil and more neglect than modern hybrid tea roses, in keeping with its heritage as a tough antique Centifolia hybrid. Introduced in France in 1845, it bears very large, very double, globular flowers in a rich rose-pink that open wide and fragrant as they mature, carried on a robust, arching shrub. Like other Centifolia-type roses it blooms once in a spectacular late-spring flush and then rests for the remainder of the season, but is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy. Needs only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering to stay vigorous and well-shaped.

common_name: Tour de Malakoff Rose (Antique Magenta-to-Violet-Gray Centifolia)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Tour de Malakoff, introduced in 1856, is a Centifolia rose famed for its large, loosely double flowers that shift from magenta-purple through violet to smoky gray-lilac as they age.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun, with room for its vigorous, somewhat lax canes to arch; Tour de Malakoff tolerates leaner soil and more neglect than modern hybrid tea roses, in keeping with its heritage as a tough antique Centifolia. Introduced in 1856, it bears large, loosely double flowers that open a vivid magenta-purple and gradually shift through violet tones to a smoky gray-lilac as they age, an unusual color transformation combined with a strong, rich fragrance. Like other Centifolia-type roses it blooms once in a heavy late-spring flush and then rests for the remainder of the season, but is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy. Light support or underplanting helps keep the heavy flowers from touching the ground; prune only to remove dead or crossing wood after flowering.

common_name: Robert le Diable Rose (Antique Multicolor Gallica-Centifolia)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Robert le Diable is an old French rose of uncertain precise origin, grown for its unusual flowers that mix purple, red, slate-gray, and violet tones.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Robert le Diable tolerates leaner soil and more neglect than modern hybrid tea roses, in keeping with its heritage as a tough antique French rose. Its compact, somewhat sprawling bush bears richly fragrant, double flowers in an unusual and variable mix of purple, crimson-red, slate-gray, and violet tones, often shifting within a single bloom as it ages. Like other old European roses of its type, it flowers once in a heavy late-spring flush and then rests for the remainder of the season, but is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy. Needs only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering to stay vigorous and well-shaped.
